citation: Plotkin, D.L.; Roberts, M.D.; Haun, C.T.; Schoenfeld, B.J. (2021). Muscle Fiber Type Transitions with Exercise Training: Shifting Perspectives. Sports.
population: Recreationally trained physical education students, male sprinters, novice runners, competitive bodybuilders, sedentary controls, and twin pairs with divergent training histories (endurance-trained vs sedentary).
intervention: Resistance training (>70% 1RM), sprint training, combined ballistic/plyometric plus strength training, stretch-shortening cycle training, and marathon training (13 weeks plus taper).
outcome_measures: Myosin heavy chain (MHC) isoform distribution via muscle homogenate SDS-PAGE
Single-fiber MHC isoform analysis via SDS-PAGE
summary: This narrative review evaluates muscle fiber identification techniques and synthesizes longitudinal and cross-sectional evidence on fiber type transitions with resistance, power, sprint, and endurance training. It emphasizes that single-fiber analysis is required to detect hybrid fibers (co-expressing multiple MHC isoforms) and that training-specific shifts occur: resistance and sprint training increase type IIa at the expense of IIx and type I, while endurance training increases type I and oxidative hybrids. The magnitude of shift appears smaller in already well-trained individuals.
key_findings: Six weeks of maximal strength training in recreationally trained students shifted triceps brachii MHC from 33.4% IIx to 19.5% (p < 0.01) and increased IIa from 49.4% to 66.7% (p < 0.01), with no change in type I proportion.
Combined ballistic/plyometric plus strength training increased IIa from 47.7% to 62.7% (p < 0.05) and decreased type I from 18.2% to 9.2% (p < 0.05) in the same cohort.

Eight weeks of sprint training in male sprinters increased vastus lateralis type IIa from 35% to 52% (p < 0.05), decreased type I from 52% to 41% (p < 0.05), and reduced IIa/IIx hybrids from 13% to 5% (p < 0.05).

Thirteen weeks of marathon training in novice runners increased vastus lateralis type I from 42.6% to 48.6%, increased I/IIa hybrids from 5.1% to 8.2%, decreased IIa from 40.1% to 35.8%, and decreased IIa/IIx hybrids from 11.9% to 6.4%.

Competitive bodybuilders possessed ~35% type I fibers versus ~48% in controls (p < 0.05), similar IIa (~45% both), but markedly higher pure IIx (~15% vs ~5%, p < 0.05), challenging the typical IIx-to-IIa shift seen in shorter-term resistance training studies.
limitations: The review is non-systematic and includes studies with heterogeneous methodologies (homogenate vs single-fiber analysis), small sample sizes, and varying training histories. Biopsy sampling variability and undefined fiber counts needed to detect shifts limit quantitative synthesis across studies.
